column3: It directly links spending good with seeking Allah and says its return is for the giver.
A reachable object tests concealed fear; it only indirectly frames costly restraint.
It distinguishes material offering from the taqwa that reaches Allah, sharpening 3:92's goal.
It identifies restrained poor recipients and affirms Allah's knowledge of every good spent.
Its acceptance and loss contrast is too general to clarify giving from what is loved.
Attaining good here concerns defeated opponents, a contrary use of the wording.
It confirms that expenditure in Allah's way is fully repaid and not wronged.
Choosing blindness over guidance supplies only a distant contrast to reaching birr.
It uses reaching for mercy, not the expenditure or birr relation of 3:92.
It names family and vulnerable people as recipients of expenditure from good.
Allah's independence and the able pilgrimage obligation offer only a general cost-bearing parallel.
It contrasts attainment of Allah's covenant by excluding wrongdoers, not giving.
It makes spending a differentiating act and places possessions under Allah's ultimate inheritance.
It directs private exchange toward birr and taqwa, preserving birr beyond material giving.
It gives a contrary instance of people being reached by wrath and humiliation.
The command to withhold support is a contrary posture toward the spending assumed in 3:92.
Allah's lack of will for injustice adds no distinct element to the verse's giving condition.
Earned shares and seeking Allah's bounty only loosely bear on relinquishing what is loved.
Honor and nearness in this announcement do not clarify expenditure or birr.
It presents secret and open spending from provision alongside worship and hoped-for return.
The nearby call adds no clear interpretive element.
Love of the immediate is a cautionary contrast to releasing loved possessions.
It grounds all good in Allah's hand but does not address the giver's release.
Its clarified boundaries of taqwa only generally relate to the verse's moral horizon.
Worldly enjoyment is a contrast to attachment, though not specifically to expenditure.
It requires the well-provided to give to kin, needy, and emigrants, even amid grievance.
Its plea to die among the abrār only echoes the root of birr without defining its path.
It tests claimed love through following, a secondary lens on love in 3:92.
Divine knowledge of inner whispering only broadly supports the inward dimension of giving.
Refusal to love sincere counsel is only a lexical, contrary parallel.
Teaching and devotion add no distinct element to the expenditure condition.
It contrasts desire for worldly gain with desire for the hereafter, qualifying attachment.
The list of earlier deniers has no clear relation to 3:92.
Sincere calling under danger and gratitude offer a remote orientation of devotion.
A vowed, dedicated child provides a secondary model of releasing what is dearly held.
The demanded pledge over a son is not an instruction about giving or birr.
Entry in peace adds no distinct element.
Inheritance distribution concerns transferred property but not voluntary expenditure.
Shared divine favor and brotherhood only broadly frame the social good of giving.
Calling on Allah as al-Barr echoes birr but does not explain its condition here.
Harvest imagery is a remote material parallel, not evidence for the verse's demand.
Fair debt practice protects property rights; it is adjacent but not voluntary release.
It counts every small or large expenditure among deeds for which Allah recompenses.
It explicitly makes giving wealth despite love of it part of birr, directly unpacking 3:92.
It names intense love of good, illuminating the costly object that 3:92 requires one to spend.
Allah's knowledge of every seed only generally parallels His knowledge of what is given.
The reversal of mockery adds no clear element.
Choosing an inferior thing over better is a remote contrast to valuing good rightly.
Its warning to People of the Book does not clarify the verse.
Guidance by stars adds no distinct element to expenditure or birr.
The hereafter being better than worldly enjoyment indirectly challenges worldly attachment.
Doubt about messengers adds no clear element.
Near repentance is a moral alternative but not a reading of giving what one loves.
A decreed share reaching deniers is a contrary use of reaching, not positive support.
The peace exemption has no distinct connection to the verse.
It commands spending in Allah's way and joins it to ihsan, reinforcing active beneficence.
The record of the abrār only echoes birr without specifying expenditure.
It commands spending from wholesome earnings and produce, and rejects giving inferior goods.
The ruined garden image adds no clear element without its surrounding context.
Allah's dislike of betrayal only negatively frames the integrity absent from sincere giving.
The marriage prohibition adds no clear element.
It affirms Allah's knowledge of every expenditure and vow, supporting accountable release.
The description of a transgressing sinner is only a general moral contrast.
It says good advanced for oneself is found with Allah, closely explaining the promised result.
Protecting an orphan's property is adjacent to wealth ethics but not charitable expenditure.
Wealth and children cannot avail before Allah, qualifying attachment to possessions.
Forgetting Allah and thereby oneself contrasts with spending that benefits one's own self.
It preserves birr, taqwa, and reconciliation as goods that should not be obstructed.
It requires justice for vulnerable orphans and affirms Allah's knowledge of every good done.
It authorizes birr and equity toward non-hostile outsiders, extending the moral field of birr.
Its refusal to feed from Allah's provision is a direct contrary response to the call to spend.
Allah's accounting of concealed and disclosed selves only generally supports inward sincerity.
Knowledge of corrupters adds no distinct element.
Repaying what spouses spent concerns restitution, not the charitable release in 3:92.
The denial of demonic descent adds no clear element.
Unequal love in a hostile relation does not clarify spending loved possessions.
Releasing or retaining spouses honorably is a distant, non-financial parallel of not harming.
The divorce resolve adds no clear element.
It warns that what people love may be harmful, qualifying love as a measure of good.
Renunciation for monotheism is a costly separation, but not an expenditure reading.
Mutual love of Allah is joined with striving and fearlessness, a secondary orientation for love.
It portrays expenditure in Allah's way as multiplied growth, supplementing the return theme.
Human love cannot itself guide; it only indirectly limits the significance of attachment.
Requital for truthfulness only broadly supports sincerity in moral action.
Failure to value Allah properly is a remote contrast to releasing His provision.
Sacrificial and compensatory offerings are ritual expenditure but do not explain loved possessions.
It commands giving from Allah's wealth to those seeking release, a secondary concrete spending case.
Mandatory inheritance shares differ from voluntary spending and add little after related cards.
The ban on reclaiming marital gifts is a narrow property-ethics parallel.
It warns that reproach, injury, and showing off nullify charity, qualifying the required spending.
Disavowal of disobedient acts adds no distinct element.
Zakah and a good loan to Allah are covenantal acts linked to forgiveness and gardens.
Inheritance obligations distribute wealth but do not interpret voluntary spending from loved things.
The command to taqwa is too general to add to 3:92.
Its monotheism judgment adds no distinct element.
The light parable and guidance do not clarify this verse's expenditure condition.
Fair measure and not diminishing others' goods give a neighboring norm of wealth justice.
Trust in Allah adds no distinct element.
Humility toward believers is a general beneficent posture, not a reading of expenditure.
This bare grouping statement adds no clear element.
Spending from bestowed provision supplies the early general frame for the command in 3:92.
It urges spending before a day when exchange and intercession fail, adding urgency.
It preserves the value of spending by forbidding reminders and injury afterward.
It depicts spending sought for Allah's pleasure and inner firmness, clarifying sincere release.
The threat of poverty explains a counter-pressure against spending loved possessions.
It distinguishes open charity from concealed charity, adding a practice of giving to the poor.
It commends spending by night and day, secretly and openly, extending the pattern of release.
Remitting a debt to one in hardship gives a non-cash form of relinquishing a valued claim.
It explicitly identifies the God-conscious as those who spend in ease and hardship.
Its ruined-expenditure image warns that wrongdoing can nullify the benefit of what is spent.
It requires a share for relatives, orphans, and the needy at property division.
It gives the contrary case of spending for people to see rather than for Allah.
It asks what loss there would be in belief and spending from Allah's provision.
Secret counsel is made good when it enjoins charity, kindness, or reconciliation.
It joins birr with taqwa as cooperative goods, broadening birr's active social form.
Feeding the needy as expiation shows a concrete transfer of valued provision.
It commands giving the harvest's due on its day, linking produce and obligatory release.
The warning against hoarded gold and silver supplies a direct contrary to generous expenditure.
Hoarded wealth becomes a consequence for its holders, reinforcing the danger of retention.
It contrasts accepted expenditure with giving done reluctantly and without faith.
It calls certain expenditures means of nearness and of the Messenger's prayers.
Taking charity is linked to cleansing and purifying its givers.
Allah's receiving of charity clarifies the divine horizon of what is given.
It frames wealth and selves as exchanged with Allah, a maximal form of release.
It pairs patience, prayer, and spending secretly and openly in seeking the final abode.
It calls believers to spend secretly and openly before the final day.
Its command to give to near kin gives a central social expression of ihsan and birr.
It directs giving the relative, needy, and traveler their due, while rejecting waste.
It rejects both clenched retention and total overextension, qualifying the manner of giving.
It identifies believers who spend from provision among the humble and steadfast.
Its sacrificial instruction includes feeding the contented and needy from what is offered.
It identifies believers by their active commitment to zakah.
It gives relatives, needy people, and travelers their due and calls this best for Allah's face.
It contrasts usury with zakah sought for Allah's face and names the latter as multiplied.
It joins hope, fear, and spending from provision as a pattern of devotion.
It promises replacement for what is spent, directly reinforcing the release of valued goods.
It includes spending from provision among the traits of a responsive community.
It warns that withholding when called to spend is self-harm, while Allah is free of need.
It joins true faith with striving by wealth and selves.
It recognizes a known share in wealth for the asker and deprived person.
It commands spending from what people hold only as successors, undercutting possessiveness.
The good loan to Allah gives expenditure a reciprocal, divine-facing form.
It joins charitable men and women with the good loan and promised multiplication.
It directs wealth's circulation so it does not remain confined among the rich.
It defines the profitable commitment as faith and striving with wealth and selves.
It commands spending for one's own good and warns against the soul's greed.
It promises multiplied return and forgiveness for a good loan to Allah.
It orders spending according to means, grounding the command in actual provision.
It identifies the righteous as those with a recognized share in their wealth.
It specifies that recognized share as due to the asker and deprived.
It pairs prayer with zakah and a good loan to Allah.
It explicitly describes feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite love for the food.
Feeding during severe hunger presents costly aid as part of the difficult ascent.
It specifies an orphaned near relative as a recipient in that difficult ascent.
It specifies a destitute person in dust as a recipient in that difficult ascent.
Giving and guarding oneself are set as the opening movement toward ease.
It describes one who gives wealth to purify himself, closely aligning giving and moral attainment.
It excludes repayment of a prior favor, sharpening the non-transactional motive of giving.
It joins sincere worship with prayer and zakah as the upright religion.
Its failure to urge feeding the poor is a direct contrary to the social release in 3:92.
